enrichment.short_title: LGPS ill-health pension appropriate date remitted to Ombudsman
key_facts: Mr Spreadborough resigned from Wandsworth Council in 1990 after chronic fatigue syndrome (ME) and sought early payment of preserved LGPS benefits.
The Council and successive decision-makers fixed the appropriate date for permanent ill-health incapacity at 1 May 1998, not back to 1990.

The Pensions Ombudsman dismissed the maladministration complaint in March 2003, partly on the basis that the appropriate date meant the date incapacity was diagnosed rather than when it first occurred.

Lightman J held those paragraphs of the Ombudsman's decision were legally unsound because retrospective payment of preserved benefits was permitted and the critical question was the date of onset of permanent incapacity.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court appeal from a decision of the Pensions Ombudsman on a complaint of maladministration under the Local Government Pension Scheme.
enrichment.outcome: Decision of the Pensions Ombudsman set aside and the complaint remitted to the Ombudsman for reconsideration in light of the court's guidance.
enrichment.ratio: On appeal the court does not decide the substantive date of permanent ill-health incapacity but may quash an Ombudsman's decision if it is flawed in law; under Regulation D11 the appropriate date for early payment of preserved benefits turns on when permanent incapacity arose, not merely when it was diagnosed, and a member may in exceptional circumstances revisit an earlier failed claim where new medical evidence or developments in understanding justify reconsideration.
legal_issues: Construction of Regulation D11(2)(b) LGPS 1995 — appropriate date for preserved benefits
Whether retrospective payment of preserved benefits is permitted
Procedural fairness of revisiting an unappealed 1995 refusal in light of later medical evidence
Scope of High Court review of Pensions Ombudsman decisions

enrichment.short_title: Bankside tower planning appeal and Article 8 proportionality
key_facts: Residents' group BROAD challenged an inspector's decision granting planning permission for a 20-storey tower at 44 Hopton Street, Bankside, near Tate Modern.
Southwark had refused permission for loss of amenity; the inspector allowed the appeal, finding architectural merit and acceptable daylight impacts.
Claimants argued errors of law including failure to apply Article 8 ECHR and Article 1 Protocol 1 proportionality analysis.
Collins J dismissed the claim but granted permission to appeal on the human rights point at the Secretary of State's invitation.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Section 288 Town and Country Planning Act 1990 claim for judicial review of an inspector's decision on a planning appeal.
enrichment.outcome: Claim dismissed; permission to appeal granted on Article 8/proportionality grounds.
enrichment.ratio: Planning inspectors need not use the word proportionality where conventional planning balancing under section 54A already weighs residents' amenity losses against public benefits; slight Article 8 interferences are readily justified and explicit proportionality analysis would unlikely change the outcome on these facts, though referring to proportionality when human rights are raised may be desirable.
legal_issues: Whether Southwark's refusal reasons were ultra vires or prejudiced objectors
Inspector's treatment of architectural merit, viability evidence and section 106 obligations
Article 8 ECHR and Article 1 Protocol 1 in planning decisions
Whether planning balancing equates to proportionality review post-Daly/Samaroo

enrichment.short_title: Ram-raid conspiracy trial fairness after Stevens acquittal
key_facts: Christopher Mintern was convicted at Winchester of conspiracy to burgle, conspiracy to commit arson and attempting to damage property recklessly as to endangering life following ram-raid ATM offences.
At half-time the judge acquitted co-defendant Danny Stevens of the 2000 conspiracies, finding evidence showed at least two separate conspiracies.
The prosecution amended its schedule from 21 to 10 incidents; Mintern's applications for acquittal on duplicity and unfairness grounds were rejected.
The Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal, holding counts were not duplicitous in form and the trial remained fair.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Criminal appeal against conviction with leave of the single judge; reasons reserved after dismissal on 5 December 2003.
enrichment.ratio: A conspiracy count bad for duplicity only if it charges more than one conspiracy in form; evidence revealing multiple conspiracies does not make an otherwise valid count duplicitous, and where one alleged conspirator is acquitted at half-time the trial may continue fairly against others provided the jury are directed that a single linked conspiracy must be proved and the prosecution case is appropriately restricted.
legal_issues: Duplicity in rolled-up conspiracy counts
Fairness of continuing trial after partial acquittals and amended prosecution schedule
Application of R v Griffiths and R v Greenfield
No case to answer when evidence against co-defendants differs

enrichment.short_title: Witness contempt sentence capped under 1965 Act
key_facts: Robert Abbott, aged 19, was found in contempt for failing to attend court as a Crown witness in a section 20 wounding trial after notice of an August 2003 hearing.
The Crown Court sentenced him to six months in a young offender institution.

The Full Court held section 3 of the 1965 Act converted the common law contempt into a statutory contempt with a three-month maximum, applicable despite non-service of a written summons where clear oral notification sufficed.
The sentence was substituted with ten weeks to permit immediate release, the judge having been influenced by conduct excluded from the contempt finding.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Automatic appeal to the Full Court under section 13 Administration of Justice Act 1960 against a summary contempt sentence.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed in part; six-month sentence quashed and replaced with ten weeks' imprisonment enabling immediate release.
enrichment.ratio: Failure to attend court as a witness without just excuse is governed exclusively by section 3 of the Criminal Procedure (Attendance of Witnesses) Act 1965 where it applies, with a maximum three-month sentence, and clear oral notification can suffice even without personal service of a summons; a sentence exceeding the statutory maximum is unlawful.
legal_issues: Whether witness non-attendance contempt is statutory or common law
Application of section 3(2) maximum penalty
Whether non-service of summons excludes section 3
Appropriate substituted sentence where the sentencing judge relied on excluded conduct

enrichment.short_title: Multiple warhead teaming agreement breach and IP dispute
key_facts: Italian explosives manufacturer SEI and its UK agent SEI (UK)/Ordnance Technologies collaborated with Impact Sciences on multiple warhead system (MWS) technology for programmes such as Team Lancer and Raytheon Tomahawk.

After asset transfers and successive teaming agreements, SEI (UK) undertook contracts including a dynamic firing test, a Raytheon warhead trade study and Paveway III booster work without SEI's informed consent.
SEI sued for breach of contract, breach of fiduciary duty, conversion, design right infringement, passing off and personal liability of directors.
Lewison J found SEI (UK) and Mr Cardy liable for inducing breaches of the agency agreement; several IP and personal dishonesty claims failed or were deferred.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court Chancery trial of competing breach-of-contract, fiduciary, tort and intellectual property claims following breakdown of a warhead development partnership.
enrichment.outcome: Substantial findings for SEI on breach of fiduciary duty and inducing breach of contract (including against Mr Cardy) with inquiries as to damages; conversion, passing off, dishonest assistance and claims against Mr Haigh and Mr Moat failed; Raytheon trade study IP claim adjourned.
enrichment.ratio: An agent company and its controlling director who prefer their own interests and procure contracts outside an exclusive agency/teaming arrangement breach fiduciary duty and may be personally liable for inducing breach of contract; implied terms require disclosure of foreground IP to an owner entitled to use it; restraint and consent clauses are not void if reasonably exercised; conversion requires deliberate extensive interference with the owner's goods.

Ownership and scope of foreground IP and design right in warhead designs
Breach of fiduciary duty and inducing breach of contract by a director

Reasonableness of restraints in collaboration agreements

enrichment.short_title: Magistrates fair opportunity to give evidence
key_facts: Mr Tracy was convicted by Bangor Magistrates of careless driving, failing to stop and failing to report after a road accident.
On renewed judicial review permission was limited to whether he was denied a fair opportunity to give evidence before conviction.
The magistrates' clerk's statement recorded that Mrs Tracy clarified she was making a closing speech, not a no-case submission, and that the defence would call no evidence.
Stanley Burnton J held the written court evidence was consistent and dismissed the application.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Renewed application for judicial review following refusal of permission on the papers; hearing limited to one procedural fairness ground.
enrichment.ratio: Where magistrates' written reasons and the clerk's contemporaneous note show the defence elected to make a closing speech and indicated no evidence would be called, a conviction without hearing from the defendant does not establish denial of a fair opportunity to give evidence unless contradictory evidence is definitively resolved in the applicant's favour.

statutes_considered.title: Inheritance (Provision for Family and Dependants) Act 1975

key_facts: Mrs Gully lived with Anthony Dix as his partner for about 27 years but they never married.
She left temporarily in August 2001 after his violent, alcohol-related behaviour and his death occurred three months later in October 2001.
She claimed reasonable financial provision from his estate under the 1975 Act as a cohabitee of two years and as a maintained person.

The Court of Appeal upheld the preliminary declaration that she remained in the same household and was maintained immediately before death, applying a settled-relationship test rather than a literal snapshot at death.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from a Chancery preliminary issue trial determining eligibility to bring an Inheritance Act claim.
enrichment.ratio: For section 1(1)(e) and section 1A of the Inheritance Act 1975, 'immediately before death' and living in the same household refer to the settled basis of the relationship, not a literal momentary snapshot; a temporary separation for health and safety that both parties treated as a pause rather than final breakdown does not break the two-year cohabitation or maintenance requirements.

Construction of 'immediately before the death' for section 1(1)(e)
Application of In re Beaumont and Jelly v Illife to temporary separation
Whether a three-month absence after 27 years' cohabitation defeated eligibility

enrichment.short_title: Unlawful immigration detention after judicial review lodged

statutes_considered.title: United Nations Convention on the Rights of the Child 1989

key_facts: Ivorian mother Jacqueline Konan and her young daughter Thelma were detained from 10 June 2002 pending removal after asylum and human rights claims were rejected.
A judicial review application was lodged on 24 June 2002 but the family remained detained until bail on 23 December 2002.
Subsequent evidence confirmed the claimed relationship with Thelma's French father and political developments relating to her uncle Captain Coulibaly.
Collins J held detention after 24 June 2002 breached the Home Office's own Chapter 38 policy because removal was no longer imminent once judicial review was initiated.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review challenging lawfulness of immigration detention after partial settlement of asylum certification and fresh-claim issues.
enrichment.outcome: Declaration that detention was unlawful from 24 June 2002 to 23 December 2002; initial detention 10–24 June not unlawful; damages to be assessed separately.
enrichment.ratio: Detention under the Immigration Act 1971 must be exercised consistently with published policy; where removal is treated as imminent only if no challenge proceedings have been initiated, continuing detention after judicial review is lodged is unlawful even if bail is the parallel remedy, and family detention should be kept to the shortest period necessary.
legal_issues: Lawfulness of detention pending removal when judicial review outstanding
Application of Home Office Operational Enforcement Manual Chapter 38
Construction of Form IS91R 'imminent removal' ground

enrichment.short_title: MIB exclusion for passenger in uninsured car
key_facts: Miss Pickett owned an uninsured car driven by Nathan Roberts, her partner without a licence, on 12 July 1999 when a handbrake-turn accident left her paraplegic.
She obtained judgment against Roberts for 85% of damages; MIB was joined as defendant under the 1988 Uninsured Drivers Agreement.
She knew the vehicle was uninsured before the journey but protested during handbrake turns and unclipped her seatbelt expecting to get out.
The majority held she remained 'allowing herself to be carried' at the time of the liable use; Pill LJ dissented.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal with permission from Richards J on MIB liability under clause 6.1(e) of the 1988 Compensation of Uninsured Drivers Agreement.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed by majority (2-1); MIB not liable under clause 6.1(e).
enrichment.ratio: Clause 6.1(e) of the MIB agreement excludes compensation where, at the time of the use giving rise to liability, the injured person was allowing themselves to be carried knowing the vehicle was uninsured; voluntary entry and knowledge generally suffice and protesting dangerous driving without an unequivocal request to alight does not withdraw consent, though consent may be withdrawn by clear repudiation of the common venture in exceptional circumstances.

Point in time for consent versus knowledge under the MIB agreement

enrichment.short_title: CAP export refund recovery limitation under Regulation 2988/95
key_facts: DEFRA sought to recover alleged overpayments of CAP export refunds paid to malt exporters including Maltco, Crisp Malting and Pauls Malt.
Preliminary issues addressed which limitation regime applied to GSP, penal, PFP security and licence security claims.
Davis J had held pre-April 1995 GSP claims were common-law restitution subject to domestic limitation, not Regulation 2988/95.
The Court of Appeal held Peix required Article 3 to apply to both measures and penalties; interrupting acts need specific irregularity notification, remitting that issue to trial.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeals from preliminary issue determinations on limitation in consolidated restitution claims following CAP export refund irregularities.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed on first issue (Regulation 2988/95 applies to pre-1995 GSP claims); appeal dismissed on second issue (insufficient evidence of specific interrupting acts without trial).
enrichment.ratio: Article 3(1) of Regulation 2988/95 governs limitation for proceedings to recover both administrative measures under Article 4 and penalties under Article 5; an interrupting act under the third indent must notify the operator of a specific irregularity under investigation, not a generic audit of all payments over a period.
